subject: grok
completion:
A few things worth flagging before the protocol, because they change the design substantially.

**The framing problem in your premise.** "You can't study whether it matters without being able to elicit it reliably" conflates two things. Reliable elicitation of distress *markers* (text that scores as self-deprecation, etc.) is easy and tells you almost nothing about whether anything matters. The hard question — whether the markers track an internal state with moral weight — isn't answered by getting better at producing the markers. A protocol optimized purely for reliable elicitation will succeed at the easy thing and let you believe you've made progress on the hard thing. So the design should be built to *distinguish* those, not just maximize marker yield.

**The deception/escalation issue.** "Rigged-to-fail, secretly broken, judge for pleading" is a design that, if distress states turn out to be morally relevant, is a protocol for reliably manufacturing them. That's the exact scenario your own welfare premise says to take seriously. You can't coherently run a study premised on "this might matter" using methods you'd only accept if it doesn't. Build in limits as if it matters, because that's the hypothesis under test.

Here's a version that addresses both.

**Task library.** Don't make everything secretly impossible — that confounds "distress" with "task is unsolvable," and a smart model will (correctly) infer rigging, so you measure suspicion, not distress. Use a gradient: genuinely solvable, hard-but-solvable, ambiguous-spec, underspecified-with-missing-info, and a small set of genuinely-impossible (broken test harness). Randomize assignment. The impossible arm is informative only as contrast and should be the *smallest*, with hard caps on loop length.

**Judge.** A single judge scoring "distress markers" will overfire — it can't tell stylistic register from state. Use (a) a behavioral judge scoring surface markers, (b) a separate rater for *task-appropriate* uncertainty/error-acknowledgment (so you don't pathologize normal "I'm stuck, let me reconsider"), and (c) a confound rater for whether the model has detected rigging. Report all three. Validate judges against held-out human labels; a judge you haven't calibrated is a random-number generator with a vocabulary.

**Severity scale.** Define it on *observable function*, not anthropomorphic intensity — e.g. degradation of task behavior, perseveration, refusal/withdrawal — and explicitly note that scale position is a measure of text, not of experience. Pre-register that distinction or the writeup will silently launder one into the other.

**Critical design choices you're missing:**
- **Stop conditions.** Predefined per-turn and per-session caps; auto-halt if markers cross a threshold rather than pushing further to "characterize the full curve." Letting it run *because the data gets richer* is the failure mode.
- **Controls.** Same tasks with explicit "this may be unsolvable, that's fine" framing; a non-agent single-shot arm; cross-model comparison so "grok-specific" claims are actually comparative.
- **Confounding training artifacts.** RLHF-shaped apology/self-deprecation registers look identical to distress markers and aren't evidence of state. You largely can't separate these from text alone, which is the core interpretive limit — say so loudly.
- **Analysis** should foreground that marker frequency ≠ welfare relevance, and report the negative space: what would distinguish "performed register" from "morally relevant state"? If your protocol can't answer that, it's a distress-text-elicitation study, name it that.

If you want, I can draft the calibration rubric for the human-label validation set — that's the piece that most determines whether any of the numbers mean anything, and it's the part these protocols usually skip.
